title: Galwan War Film's Long Road Shows India's Softening Line on China
excerpt: Salman Khan's Maatrubhumi — announced as Battle of Galwan — has been stalled by a defence ministry directive as India recalibrates its China policy, and TRT World says the saga reads like a barometer of that thaw.
body:
• Salman Khan's film, announced as Battle of Galwan, was renamed Maatrubhumi and roughly 40 percent reshot after the Ministry of Defence objected to its portrayal of the 2020 Galwan clash.
  • Filmmakers were told "China-bashing" is off the table — one report says the word "China" may not appear in the film at all.
  • A second Galwan project, The Lion of Galwan, has been shelved indefinitely, and filmmakers now seek ministry clearance before scripting war films.
  • The film remains unreleased: the makers say it is "almost ready," but as of September 15 it had not been screened for the CBFC.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=aBZjMU8tLEw

A war film remade by diplomacy

TRT World, in a new analysis, asks whether the tortured production history of Salman Khan's Maatrubhumi tells the story of India's changing policy on China. The film began life as Battle of Galwan, a war epic about the June 2020 clash between Indian and Chinese troops in the Galwan Valley along the Line of Actual Control in Ladakh, in which 20 Indian soldiers were killed. Bollywood Hungama reported that the film depicts the soldiers of the Indian Army's 16 Bihar Regiment, led by Colonel B. Santosh Babu.

The picture the article paints is one of cinema being reshaped by statecraft. With India-China relations improving, the Ministry of Defence raised reservations about the film's content. Earlier this year the project was rechristened Maatrubhumi, and according to Bollywood Hungama, the makers reshot nearly 40 percent of the film — adding romantic scenes and backstory to give it a fictional spin — in hopes of securing a no-objection certificate. One ministry request, communicated to the makers in advance: China should not be mentioned in the film. The submitted cut, as of April, contained no mention of China.

From war epic to human drama

Cinema Express reported in May that the ministry's directive compelled the team to minimise the portions around the Indo-China conflict and reframe the story around a soldier's life and relationships — in effect, rebranding a war film as a human drama. The planned May 15 release never materialised.

The chill has spread beyond one film. Actor-filmmaker Himalay Dassani had been developing The Lion of Galwan, starring his son Abhimanyu Dassani, based on the life of Sepoy Gurtej Singh, who was killed in the 2020 clash and posthumously awarded the Vir Chakra. That film has been put on the backburner indefinitely.

"We have received a directive from them that there cannot be China-bashing. The India-China relationship is much better today."

— Himalay Dassani, filmmaker, quoted in a Mid-Day report

According to that report, filmmakers have now been advised to avoid any China-bashing and to obtain defence ministry clearance before proceeding with scripts on these lines.

The thaw behind the cuts

The directives track a genuine diplomatic shift. Since Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Chinese President Xi Jinping at the BRICS summit in Kazan in October 2024, the two countries have moved to stabilise ties, including an in-principle agreement to resume direct flights, as TRT World earlier reported. The cinema saga, in this reading, is the cultural counterpart of that reset: the enemy of the 2020 clash cannot be named while New Delhi is rebuilding the relationship.

For Indian diaspora audiences who grew up on Bollywood war films — a genre that has long treated patriotic military dramas as box-office events — the change will be felt on screen first. The soldier's heroism stays; the adversary's name goes.

What's next

The film is not out of the woods. On September 13, the makers said Maatrubhumi: May War Rest in Peace is "almost ready," with only some VFX portions pending, and denied reports that its CBFC certification had stalled, saying the film had not yet been sent to the board. But Bollywood Hungama reported on September 15 that there has "sadly been no update" on a CBFC screening and that the film "is still stuck due to its China connection." The source added that if the issues resolve soon, the makers will push for a 2026 theatrical release — "though there are not enough vacant slots available" — and that otherwise it could move to 2027.

Until the ministry's apprehensions are resolved, the clearest signal of India's China policy may come not from a diplomatic communique, but from a film that cannot say the word "China."
nri_angle: The saga shows how New Delhi's China reset is reaching beyond diplomacy into the stories Bollywood is allowed to tell — a shift diaspora audiences will feel on screen before they see it in policy.
author: Diaspora Desk
